title: How do you approach player retention in games? What mechanics do you use to keep players coming back?
author: Few_Paramedic_8561
selftext:
Over the past few weeks, I’ve managed to attract a fairly large number of players to my game, but I’m still struggling to build an effective retention system.  
Neither daily rewards nor the ability to build family dynasties spanning several centuries seem to be helping so far.  
I’ve already conducted several audits, but I still haven’t managed to increase my player retention rate.  
The interesting thing is that I’m getting great reviews and positive feedback. I can see that people genuinely enjoy the game. However, somewhere around day 4 or 5, they simply stop coming back.  
I’d really appreciate your advice on this. Have any of you faced similar challenges? What mechanics or strategies have worked for you when it comes to bringing players back and keeping them engaged long-term?

comments.author: lastplankgames
comments.body: It's hard to say as you've not given much details on your game. Is it mobile? What are the mechanics? etc

replies.author: Few_Paramedic_8561
replies.body:
Thanks for asking! It's a browser-based life simulation game built with HTML/JavaScript. It's playable on both desktop and mobile browsers, but it's not a native mobile app.

The concept is similar to BitLife, but with a historical twist. You can be born in different countries, historical periods, social classes and circumstances. The game spans almost 4,000 years of history.

The main mechanics include:

\- Random birth and life circumstances.

\- Making decisions that affect health, wealth, relationships, education and survival.

\- Random events, historical events and branching storylines.

\- Marriage, children and the ability to continue playing as your descendants, building a dynasty across generations.

\- Childhood activities and education that influence your future.

\- Gambling and risky decisions that can dramatically change your life.

The main idea is that every life is different, and you can potentially build a family dynasty spanning thousands of years.

Here's the game if you'd like to take a look: [https://thousands.life/](https://thousands.life/)

My biggest challenge right now isn't attracting new players, but getting them to return after the first few days. I'm trying to figure out what long-term progression systems and gameplay loops could make people genuinely invested in their dynasties.

![gif](giphy|557Ifn9WbfpSBHzoJL)

replies.author: lastplankgames
replies.body:
So browser based is hard because a player can easily close a tab when they're bored. With a steam game, they'd rather carry on sometimes due to the pain of switching games.

So playing it for a few mins, I can see that we're launched straight into options. There's no ease into gameplay or tutorial. As soon as I get in I'm making life choices. I would suggest some sort of summary screen that gives me a general overview, and then allowing me to choose the next "event". As it stands, it's a a pop up and I feel pressured to select an option. Perhaps let the user decide when their ready, and then select "next milestone" or along those lines.

replies.author: Few_Paramedic_8561
replies.body:
That’s a good idea. I’m actually also working on improving the first interaction a player has with the game, making sure they can get started smoothly, understand what they’re expected to do, and know where to find everything they need for a comfortable gaming experience.  
Previously, the game had a short tutorial, but A/B tests showed that players were skipping it quite frequently. During the audit, pop-up messages demonstrated better conversion rates, so I decided to go with that approach for now.  
However, I agree that new players should have some kind of short preview of what awaits them in the game. I’ll definitely think about that.
